🇺🇸🇨🇦 REMEMBER THE “NORTH AMERICAN TRADE WAR” PANIC?

Since April 2025, we’ve heard endless warnings about tariffs, retaliation and a U.S.–Canada trade war supposedly sending consumer prices soaring.

So more than a year later, what actually happened?

The Federal Reserve studied actual purchases from as many as 200,000 American households and found that retail prices for goods imported from Canada, Mexico and other non-China countries combined had risen only about 2.5% relative to April 2025 by December.

And even that 2.5% cannot simply be blamed on tariffs. Normal inflation, producer costs, exchange rates and other factors can also affect prices.

It gets even more interesting when Canada is isolated.

According to the Fed’s country-specific price index, Canadian goods were only about 0.6% more expensive year-over-year in December 2025. U.S.-made goods in the same dataset increased roughly 1.2%.

Think about that.

After months of freak outs, propaganda and  headlines about a massive North American “trade war,” Canadian goods in this dataset were experiencing LESS retail inflation than American-made goods.

That doesn’t mean tariffs had NO consequences. Certain industries, manufacturers and exporters have been affected.

But when it comes to one of the biggest warnings sold to the American public — “YOU are going to pay dramatically higher prices” — the measurable consumer impact has so far been remarkably modest.

A $100 basket experiencing a 2.5% increase becomes $102.50.

And remember: that 2.5% isn't even Canada alone and isn't necessarily all tariff-related.

There’s a huge difference between headline tariff rates and what ultimately shows up at the cash register.

After all the predictions, threats, retaliatory announcements and breathless headlines, it’s worth comparing the rhetoric with what consumers actually experienced.

The data tell a much less dramatic story than the headlines did.

Numbers matter.....fear porn doesn't.
